question: What is the main goal of tracking infectious diseases in public health?

options.A: Treating individual patients in rural clinics
options.B: Managing hospital budgets for drug procurement
options.C: Conducting clinical trials for new vaccines
options.D: Tracking health data to plan and evaluate prevention

explanation: You've got this! Disease tracking is all about collecting health data so we can plan ahead and stop outbreaks before they spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: Why are bedside nurses so important for disease tracking and surveillance?

options.A: They manufacture vaccines for widespread distribution
options.B: They record the initial symptom patterns during patient care
options.C: They fund laboratory testing for suspected pathogens
options.D: They write national health policies for disease control

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you are usually the first to notice unusual symptoms in a patient, making your initial observations vital for catching outbreaks early. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: Which agency coordinates national disease tracking and emergency response in Nigeria?

options.C: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration

explanation: Well done! The NCDC is Nigeria's main public health agency leading the charge on disease surveillance and emergencies. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Why is reporting certain infectious diseases a legal duty for nurses?

options.A: Hospital management requires extra paperwork for audits
options.B: Patients pay a special tax for disease registration
options.C: Public safety outweighs individual privacy during potential outbreaks
options.D: Insurers need confirmation before paying hospital bills

explanation: Exactly! Protecting the wider community from a fast-spreading outbreak comes first, which is why quick reporting is required by law. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Lassa fever and Cholera belong to which category of notifiable diseases in Nigeria?
explanation: You got it! Dangerous, epidemic-prone infections like Lassa fever and Cholera are Category 1 diseases that need urgent attention. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: A patient arrives with severe watery diarrhea in an area with a cholera outbreak. How quickly must this be reported?

options.A: Only if laboratory results return positive
options.D: By the end of the month

explanation: Spot on! Suspected cholera is an emergency—it must be reported within 24 hours to trigger rapid public health action. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do when suspecting a notifiable disease?

options.A: Publish the data on social media

explanation: Great job! Always start by informing your facility's designated surveillance officer so the official reporting chain can begin. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: Why is asking about a patient's recent travel history so important during an assessment?

options.A: It determines the patient's ability to pay hospital bills
options.B: It helps link symptoms to localized disease outbreaks elsewhere
options.C: It replaces the need for laboratory diagnostic tests
options.D: It fulfills routine clerical admission requirements

explanation: Brilliant! Knowing where a patient has traveled gives you crucial clues if they've picked up an infection active in another region. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: Who is the primary contact person at the Local Government level for disease notification?
explanation: You nailed it! The DSNO at the LGA level is your go-to person for receiving initial facility health reports. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the correct reporting pathway for a disease notification in Nigeria?

options.A: Facility to LGA, then State, then NCDC
options.B: Patient to Federal Ministry, bypassing local officers
options.C: LGA straight to international health organizations
options.D: State to NCDC, then directly to the clinic

explanation: Spot on! Reports travel step-by-step from your clinic up to the LGA, then the State, and finally to the national NCDC. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of contact tracing during an infectious outbreak?

options.A: Punishing individuals who break public health quarantine rules
options.B: Collecting financial donations for hospital equipment
options.C: Identifying and monitoring people exposed to an infected person
options.D: Conducting research on chronic non-communicable diseases

explanation: Correct! Tracing contacts helps us find anyone who might have caught the infection so we can monitor them before it spreads further. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Why must contact tracing happen quickly during a viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak?

options.A: To prevent staff burnout in rural health centers
options.B: To satisfy international tourism documentation standards
options.C: To reduce the cost of laboratory chemical reagents
options.D: To isolate new cases before they infect others

explanation: Well done! Speed is everything—catching new cases fast cuts off the chain of transmission and keeps the community safe. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: What is considered the single most effective way to prevent hospital-acquired infections?
explanation: You've got this! Good hand hygiene washes away germs and is your absolute best defense against spreading infections in the ward. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: When should transmission-based precautions be started for a patient?

options.A: When an infectious disease is suspected or confirmed
options.B: At the time of discharge from the facility
options.C: When the patient requests a private hospital room
options.D: Only after laboratory cultures return positive results

explanation: Exactly! Don't wait for lab results—start precautions immediately if an infection is even suspected to keep everyone safe. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: Which of these is a common challenge for disease tracking in remote or rural areas?

options.A: Overfunding of local primary health clinics
options.B: Excessive availability of advanced diagnostic testing
options.C: Too many trained surveillance officers on duty
options.D: Poor communication tools and logistical bottlenecks

explanation: Spot on! Bad roads, poor network, and transport issues often delay urgent health reports from remote areas. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)

question: How can health workers best handle community distrust during a disease outbreak?

options.A: Ignoring local beliefs and customs entirely
options.C: Engaging local leaders and communicating transparently
options.D: Relying solely on international media broadcasts

explanation: Brilliant! Working closely with community leaders and being open and honest builds trust and encourages people to report symptoms early. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)
